extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, critics and educated readers interested in literary style and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for literary composition and social wit focused on how writing (poetry, fiction, history, description) and conversation (raillery) should be fashioned to gratify the reader's imagination and preserve agreeable social manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical liberty: mend and perfect Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the part of a Poet to humour the Imagination in its own Notions, by mending and perfecting Nature where he describes a Reality, and by adding greater Beauties than are put together in Nature, where he describes a Fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Poet may combine seasons, make different flowers bloom together, create new species, adapt soil to any climate, alter winds and rivers, and otherwise 'model' Nature to please the reader's Imagination — provided he 'does not reform her too much, and run into Absurdities, by endeavouring to excel.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairy Way of Writing: required genius and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a kind of Writing...which Mr. Dryden calls 'the Fairy Way of Writing'...more difficult than any other that depends on the Poet's Fancy, because he has no Pattern to follow in it, and must work altogether out of his own Invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success requires a particular cast of fancy (a naturally fruitful and superstitious imagination) and being 'very well versed in Legends and Fables, antiquated Romances, and the Traditions of Nurses and old Women' so as to 'fall in with our natural Prejudices' and avoid making fairies 'talk like People of his own Species.' The sense of such beings should be 'a little discoloured' to seem proper to their condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emblematical persons: personifying passions and qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors sometimes represent any Passion, Appetite, Virtue or Vice, under a visible Shape, and make it a Person or an Actor in his Poem (e.g. Hunger and Envy in Ovid; Fame in Virgil; Sin and Death in Milton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique (used notably by Spencer) allows writers to address the Imagination by giving sensible shape to intellectual faculties; it is an established poetic device and demands imaginative skill in selecting and sustaining such personifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: History and narrative: follow nature closely and unfold by degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers obliged to take entire Scenes out of Nature (Historians, natural Philosophers, Travellers, Geographers) must follow Nature more closely and take entire Scenes out of her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Historian pleases the Imagination by 'drawing up his Armies and fight his Battels in proper Expressions,' setting before our Eyes divisions, cabals, jealousies, and leading us 'Step by Step into the several Actions and Events' so the subject unfolds by just degrees, keeps the reader in pleasing suspense, and allows sympathies to form. Livy is cited as exemplary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scale and proportion to enlarge imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is more pleasant to the Fancy, than to enlarge itself by Degrees, in its Contemplation of the various Proportions its several Objects bear to each other...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers of natural philosophy and descriptive prose please imagination by presenting contrasts of scale (from green leaves swarming with invisible animals to worlds and firmaments), by telescopic discoveries, and by carrying thought into immense or minute realms — while being conscious of the imagination's limits so as not to render speculation ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of allusions: borrow from the great and known
rubrics_metrics.description: The Great Art of a Writer shews it self in the Choice of pleasing Allusions, which are generally to be taken from the great or beautiful Works of Art or Nature; the chief Design of an Allusion being to illustrate and explain the Passages of an Author, it should be always borrowed from what is more known and common, than the Passages which are to be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscure, learned comparisons drawn only from a writer's own scientific or specialized study (e.g. Chymistry or Cartesians) that a general reader won't follow; likewise avoid allusions too mean or familiar (shop-craft) for polite discourse. Prefer images from Nature and widely-known art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor and similitude: exactness or agreeableness
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble Metaphor, when it is placed to an Advantage, casts a kind of Glory round it, and darts a Lustre through a whole Sentence...the Likeness ought to be very exact, or very agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an allusion or metaphor to please the Imagination its resemblance should be precise or particularly pleasing (graceful posture/air). Ill-chosen comparisons spoil the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions: power of words and selection of proper circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Descriptions in particular. The Power of Words over the Imagination. Why one Reader more pleased with Descriptions than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good descriptive writing depends on the writer's skill in selecting the proper circumstances and particulars that form a lively picture; the same description will affect readers differently depending on their faculties and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works of Nature vs. Works of Art: comparative pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Works of Nature more pleasant to the Imagination than those of Art. The Works of Nature still more pleasant, the more they resemble those of Art. The Works of Art more pleasant, the more they resemble those of Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or choosing images, prefer those from Nature for broad delight; art that echoes natural forms heightens pleasure. In architecture and other arts, aim for greatness, beauty, or novelty to please the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: What pleases imagination in architecture: great, beautiful, or new
rubrics_metrics.description: Every thing that pleases the Imagination in Architecture is either Great, Beautiful, or New. Greatness in Architecture relates either to the Bulk or to the Manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use size (bulk) or manner (concave/convex forms that suggest grandeur) and novelty or beauty to produce imaginative effect; historical examples and oriental bulk are cited to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disagreeable or terrible descriptions can please when apt
rubrics_metrics.description: Why anything that is unpleasant to behold, pleases the Imagination when well described...Why Terror and Grief are pleasing to the Mind when excited by Descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may legitimately evoke disagreeable passions (terror, grief) because, when well described and apt, such passions can produce exquisite pleasure; skillful raising of passion heightens imaginative delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: A writer's imagination is essential to embellish good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: It is this Talent of affecting the Imagination, that gives an Embellishment to good Sense, and makes one Man's Compositions more agreeable than another's...it is the very Life and highest Perfection of Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when arguments or ideas are sound, the presence of imaginative embellishment is what renders compositions enduring and pleasing; lack of imagination makes works appear dry and insipid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of agreeable raillery (social wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: To rally well, it is absolutely necessary that Kindness must run thro' all you say, and you must ever preserve the Character of a Friend to support your Pretensions to be free with a Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to gain goodwill; avoid 'extremely sharp and biting' expressions that humiliate or wound. Good raillery forms ridicule on an excess in a laudable quality (so the person is not provoked) and often makes the person 'a Fool by his own Consent.' Preserve friendship and avoid malevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of raillery and their social effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters of raillers: Callisthenes (gentle, witty, keeps person in countenance), Acetus (merciless, causes pain and division), Minutius (self-implicating, insinuates shared faults).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulate Callisthenes' method to cement company and make people enjoy themselves; avoid Acetus's cruel mockery which creates enmity. Minutius's technique of confessing the same fault keeps the target in countenance and is socially artful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire's proper target: vice not the person
rubrics_metrics.description: The most agreeable Kind of Raillery...when the Satyr is directed against Vice, with an Air of Contempt of the Fault, but no Ill-will to the Criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satirical depiction (e.g., Congreve's Doris) can expose immoral behavior while preserving an overall genial or generous tone so the work criticizes fault without vindictive personal attack.
